title: Electrical Safety in the Laboratory

references.label: Biosafety in Microbiological and Biomedical Laboratories (BMBL)

summary: Practices for using electrical laboratory equipment (centrifuges, water baths, heating equipment, power supplies) safely, including around the wet or humid conditions common in a lab.
explanation: Laboratories regularly combine electrical equipment with liquids, humid environments (e.g. near water baths and autoclaves), and high-power devices (electrophoresis power supplies, heating mantles), which raises the risk of shock, arc flash, or equipment-triggered fire relative to a typical office setting. Basic controls — keeping liquids away from outlets and cords, inspecting equipment and cords before use, and never bypassing a device's grounding or safety interlocks — address most of this risk.
keyPractices: Inspect power cords and plugs for fraying, cracking, or exposed wire before use, and take damaged equipment out of service.
Keep liquids away from outlets, power strips, and cords; use spill trays under equipment near wet work when appropriate.
Never bypass a ground pin, safety interlock, or fuse rating to get a piece of equipment working.
Unplug equipment before performing maintenance, cleaning, or clearing a jam, unless the manufacturer's procedure specifically states otherwise.

Be aware that high-voltage equipment (e.g. gel electrophoresis power supplies) can deliver dangerous shocks even at relatively low current — never touch an electrophoresis chamber while it is running.
commonMistakes: Running an electrophoresis power supply with the lid open or reaching into a running gel chamber.
Using a damaged cord or an ungrounded adapter to work around a broken plug.
Placing water baths, ice buckets, or other liquid containers directly next to unprotected outlets or power strips.
